output.brief: The yield drop (41.8% to 34.3%) is mostly explained by the cut to merit awards, not by the Admissions Office. Yield fell only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's went from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield stayed flat (36.6% to 36.2%). Students with no merit award were nearly flat (38.5% to 37.0%). Early-action students, who were processed on the old system and on time, saw yield fall almost as much (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular-decision students (39.0% to 31.5%). So slow decisions do not explain most of the loss. The applicant pool was larger and slightly stronger, so a weaker pool does not explain it either. The finance committee expected a small yield effect, based on an old 2021 estimate. That estimate looks wrong. The portal delays and missing transcripts are real service problems, but their effect on yield is small and unmeasured. I am fairly confident in this, though the tier data doesn't split by round and I didn't check competitor pricing. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a decision-turnaround target and look into the transcript problem separately.
